SECTION 010:00–3:39

Turn the nullspace definition into an algorithm

Row operations preserve the solutions of Ax = 0.

Lecture 6 defined the nullspace as all inputs x satisfying Ax = 0. Lecture 7 explains how to compute that whole space, even when a matrix is rectangular and dependencies prevent a pivot in every column.

Strang’s first example is

A=[1222246836810]

Column 2 is twice column 1. Row 3 is the sum of rows 1 and 2. These relationships should emerge automatically from elimination.

Subtracting a multiple of one equation from another, exchanging equations, or scaling an equation by a nonzero number are reversible operations. They change how the system is written while preserving its solutions. A zero right-hand side stays zero throughout.

Ax = 0   →   Ux = 0   →   Rx = 0
The solution set is unchanged.
Track what is preserved

Row operations preserve the nullspace. They can change the column space as a set of output vectors.

The reduced matrices will reveal the free choices in x. Their pivot columns also identify which corresponding columns of the original matrix supply independent directions.

SECTION 023:39–6:37

Skip a column that has no available pivot

A missing pivot is a reason to move right and continue.

The first pivot is the 1 in row 1, column 1. Clear the entries beneath it:

R₂ ← R₂ − 2R₁,   R₃ ← R₃ − 3R₁.
[1222246836810]→[122200240024]

At the next stage, the prospective pivot in column 2 is zero. The entry below it is zero too, so a row exchange cannot supply a pivot in that column. Leave column 2 and move to column 3.

The 2 in row 2, column 3 is the next pivot. Subtract row 2 from row 3:

[122200240024]→[122200240000]

The result is in row echelon form: pivots form a staircase moving right as we go down, entries below each pivot are zero, and zero rows sit at the bottom. For a rectangle, the staircase description is more general than calling U upper triangular.

SECTION 036:37–9:17

Separate pivot variables from free variables

Rank counts the pivots; the other columns provide free choices.

The rank r is the number of pivots. This example has two pivots, so rank(A) = 2.

The variables corresponding to pivot columns are pivot variables. Here those columns are 1 and 3, so x₁ and x₃ are pivot variables. The other variables, x₂ and x₄, are free variables.

Pivot variables: x₁, x₃.
Free variables: x₂, x₄.

The nonzero rows of U give two equations:

x₁ + 2x₂ + 2x₃ + 2x₄ = 0,
2x₃ + 4x₄ = 0.

The last row contributes only 0 = 0. We can assign any real values to x₂ and x₄, then use back substitution to determine x₃ and x₁.

Although the original system displayed three equations, the zero row reveals a dependent equation. Only two independent constraints remain. The next two sections make convenient zero-and-one choices for the free variables.

SECTION 049:17–12:29

Set the first free variable to one

Choose x₂ = 1 and x₄ = 0, then back substitute.

Assign x₂ = 1 and x₄ = 0. The bottom nonzero equation becomes 2x₃ = 0, giving x₃ = 0. The top equation then gives x₁ + 2 = 0, so x₁ = −2.

s1=[−2100]

Check it in the original matrix:

[1222246836810][−2100]=[000]

By columns, the same calculation says −2a₁ + a₂ = 0. It expresses the dependence seen at the beginning: column 2 is twice column 1.

Every multiple cs₁ also belongs to N(A), because A(cs₁) = cAs₁ = 0. Those multiples fill a line in R⁴. However, the line does not yet describe the whole nullspace: the other free variable still has an independent choice.

SECTION 0512:29–14:52

Set the other free variable to one

Choose x₂ = 0 and x₄ = 1.

Now choose x₂ = 0 and x₄ = 1. The bottom equation is 2x₃ + 4 = 0, so x₃ = −2. Substitute upward:

x₁ + 2(−2) + 2 = 0   ⇒   x₁ = 2.
s2=[20−21]

Again check the original matrix:

[1222246836810][20−21]=[000]

In column language, 2a₁ − 2a₃ + a₄ = 0. This gives another dependence among A’s columns.

The second solution cannot be a multiple of the first: s₁ has fourth component 0, whereas s₂ has fourth component 1. Each vector turns on a different free variable.

Strang calls these special solutions because their free-variable entries are chosen systematically: one free variable is 1, and the others are 0.

SECTION 0614:52–19:03

Combine the special solutions to get every solution

There is one special solution for each free variable.

The full nullspace contains all combinations of the two special solutions:

x = cs₁ + ds₂,   c, d ∈ R.
x=c[−2100]+d[20−21]

To see why no solutions are missed, assign arbitrary free values x₂ = c and x₄ = d. Back substitution gives x₃ = −2d and x₁ = −2c + 2d. Thus

x = (−2c + 2d, c, −2d, d)ᵀ.

This is exactly cs₁ + ds₂. The two coefficients are unique because they can be read directly from x₂ and x₄. Therefore the special solutions are independent and form a basis of N(A).

The count

For an m × n matrix with rank r, there are r pivot variables and n − r free variables. The nullspace has n − r independent special solutions.

Here n = 4 and r = 2, so N(A) is two-dimensional inside R⁴. Its vectors have four components even though two parameters suffice to describe them.

Completeness written out. The explicit parameterization and uniqueness argument expand the lecture’s conclusion that the special solutions generate the entire nullspace.

SECTION 0719:03–23:00

Reduce U until each pivot column is an identity column

Clear above the pivots and scale every pivot to one.

The echelon form already solves the problem by back substitution. Strang continues to a cleaner form, the reduced row echelon form, denoted R.

Starting with U, subtract its second row from its first. This removes the 2 above the second pivot:

[122200240000]→[120−200240000]

Divide row 2 by its pivot, 2:

R=[120−200120000]

Each pivot is now 1, and its column has zeros everywhere else. The zero row remains at the bottom. Together with the echelon staircase, these are the defining conditions of reduced row echelon form.

The zero row arose because the original third row was the sum of the first two rows. Elimination exposed that dependent equation and left 0 = 0.

All operations are reversible, so N(A) = N(U) = N(R). Reducing further makes the same solution set easier to read.

SECTION 0823:00–27:43

Read the identity part and the free part

The reduced equations reveal the special solutions directly.

In R, take rows 1 and 2 and columns 1 and 3. Those entries form the two-by-two identity matrix. This is the pivot part.

The entries in the same rows but free columns 2 and 4 form

F=[2−202]

The equations Rx = 0 now read

x₁ + 2x₂ − 2x₄ = 0,
x₃ + 2x₄ = 0.

For the free assignment (x₂, x₄) = (1, 0), the pivot entries (x₁, x₃) are (−2, 0). For the assignment (0, 1), they are (2, −2).

These pivot pairs are precisely the columns of −F. The signs reverse when the free-variable terms move to the other side of the equations.

Read the equation

Pivot variables = −F × free variables. The identity pivot block makes further back substitution unnecessary.

SECTION 0927:43–33:02

Collect every special solution in a nullspace matrix

After grouping variables, the formula is N = [−F; I].

Suppose the pivot columns have been placed first. The reduced form then has a block structure:

R = [ I   F ;   0   0 ].

The pivot identity has size r × r. F has size r × (n − r), and the remaining rows, if any, are zero. With variables split into pivot and free groups,

xpivot + Fxfree = 0
⇒ xpivot = −Fxfree.

Set the free-variable part to each column of the identity. All special solutions can be assembled at once:

N = [ −F ; I ],   RN = 0.

N has n rows and n − r columns. Its columns are independent because their free-variable entries form an identity. Their combinations give every solution.

Keep track of variable order

In the numerical example the grouped order is (x₁, x₃, x₂, x₄). To state answers in the original order (x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄), restore the rows accordingly. The resulting nullspace matrix is

N=[−22100−201]

Its columns are s₁ and s₂. They satisfy AN = 0 and RN = 0 using the original column order of A and R.

Ordering and software context. The lecture explicitly supposes the pivot columns come first when introducing the blocks. The row-restoration explanation here expands that assumption. Its MATLAB and teaching-code commands are historical remarks; a software nullspace routine may return a different basis for the same space.

Apply the algorithm to the transpose

Use B = Aᵀ to distinguish the second example from the first.

For a second example, Strang transposes the original matrix and calls the new one A again. This edition calls it B = Aᵀ so the two calculations stay distinct:

B has four rows and three columns. Its column 3 is column 1 plus column 2. The first two columns are independent, so we expect two pivot columns and one free column.

This is the transpose of the row relation in the first example: its third row was the sum of its first two rows. Transposition turns that into a column dependence.

The number of pivots stays two. The lecture states the general fact that A and Aᵀ have equal rank. Their nullspaces, however, can have different dimensions because they have different numbers of columns.

SECTION 1135:05–37:37

Exchange rows when a pivot is available below

This zero pivot position can be repaired by a row exchange.

The first pivot of B is 1. Subtract twice row 1 from each lower row:

[1232462682810]→[123000022044]

The next pivot position contains zero, but unlike the first example there is a nonzero entry below it. Exchange rows 2 and 3 to bring a 2 into that position.

Now subtract twice the new row 2 from row 4. The echelon form is

UB=[123022000000]

There are two pivots, in columns 1 and 2. In column 3, all remaining possible pivot entries are zero. We have checked the last column and can stop.

Thus rank(B) = 2. Variables x₁ and x₂ are pivot variables, and x₃ is the only free variable.

Two different responses to zero

If a nonzero pivot candidate exists below, exchange rows. If every candidate in that column is zero, move to the next column.

SECTION 1237:37–40:31

Find the transpose’s one special solution

Set x₃ = 1 and back substitute through two equations.

The nonzero echelon equations for B are

x₁ + 2x₂ + 3x₃ = 0,
2x₂ + 2x₃ = 0.

Choose the free variable x₃ = 1. The lower equation gives x₂ = −1. The upper equation then becomes x₁ − 2 + 3 = 0, so x₁ = −1.

[1232462682810][−1−11]=[0000]

This is also a quick column check: minus column 1 minus column 2 plus column 3 is zero. The column dependence matches the solution coefficients.

N(B) = { c(−1, −1, 1)ᵀ : c ∈ R }.

It is a line in R³. A single vector gives a basis; the parameter c is needed to describe the entire nullspace.

Compare the examples: A and B have the same rank 2, but A has four columns and a two-dimensional nullspace, whereas B has three columns and a one-dimensional nullspace.

SECTION 1340:31–43:06

Reduce the second example and read −F again

The same block rule finishes the second calculation.

Continue from UB. Subtract its second row from its first to clear the 2 above the second pivot. Then divide row 2 by 2:

RB=[101011000000]

The pivot columns come first in this example, so the top two rows are already [I F], with F = (1, 1)ᵀ. The two zero rows impose no additional conditions.

F=[11],NB=[−1−11]

The free entry is 1, and the pivot entries are −F. This is exactly the special solution already obtained by back substitution.

The algorithm to keep

  1. Eliminate, exchanging rows or skipping columns as needed.
  2. Locate the pivot columns and the free variables.
  3. Set each free variable in turn to 1, with the others 0.
  4. Solve for the pivot variables.
  5. Take all linear combinations of the resulting special solutions.

Reducing to R makes step 4 a direct reading of the free block, with a minus sign. The lecture closes with the homogeneous problem solved; the next lecture develops the full solution of Ax = b.

Sources & editorial notes

Gilbert Strang. Lecture 7: Solving Ax = 0: pivot variables, special solutions. 18.06 Linear Algebra, Spring 2010. Massachusetts Institute of Technology: MIT OpenCourseWare. MIT identifies these original videos as recordings from Fall 1999.

This independent reading edition contains thirteen study sections, thirteen recreated mathematical figures, thirteen embedded board references, and all 690 official English caption cues. Every elimination stage and special solution was checked against the lecture board and with exact arithmetic. Original caption wording, including transcription errors and changes of matrix labels, is preserved; only paragraph layout and line wrapping change.

Study explanations and figure captions are editorial. The full two-parameter solution and its completeness argument expand the lecture’s conclusion. The second matrix is called B = Aᵀ here to distinguish it from the first A; the original spoken labels remain in the transcript. The block formula N = [−F; I] requires pivot coordinates first; the numerical example explicitly restores the original variable order. MATLAB and teaching-code comments are historical lecture context, not current software documentation.
